hypothesis: Wine starts every new process with fork(), which write-protects all of Live's private memory; after Live starts its helper processes during Set load, the first write to each 4 KiB page takes a page fault, and the first writes to a buffer when a clip first plays become ~1,500 faults inside one audio block (diagnostic D0003: the deterministic first-pass late blocks). Starting processes with posix_spawn (patch 0112, WINE_POSIX_SPAWN=1) leaves Live's memory writable, removes those late blocks and so the PipeWire errors they cause. Pre-registered with the T0004 rule plus mechanism checks.

evidence.call_site: ntdll.so spawn_process() fork() -> write-protect faults on Live's heap (vcruntime140 memcpy, Live.exe first-use copies)

hypothesis: D0003's perf data showed about 11 % of the audio threads' cycles in the kernel's RT balancing (balance_rt, pull_rt_task, double_rq_lock) while Live's AudioCalc workers sleep and wake about 53,000 times a second. A thread allowed on one CPU cannot be pushed or pulled, so pinning pipeasio-rt and each of the nine workers to a CPU of its own (instead of all of them sharing CPUs 0-11) removes that work and lowers the audio threads' CPU. Headroom campaign item 1 (user: 'Lets test all of this'); pre-registered with rule H.

hypothesis: Ableton deliberately puts one audio thread on each hyperthreaded core (user: 'Ableton intentionally allocated threads to only one core on a hyperthreaded core. Can we do that?'), but under Wine its own placement does not take effect: unpinned, its audio threads run on CPUs 0-15. T0021 forced workers onto sibling hyperthreads and saved nothing. With ABLETON_MAX_AUDIO_THREADS=5 there are six audio threads for the six physical P-cores: pipeasio-rt alone on core 0 (CPU 0) and the five AudioCalc workers alone on cores 1-5 (CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8, 10), every sibling hyperthread free of audio threads. No two audio threads then share a core's execution resources, so the audio threads use less CPU. Headroom campaign item 2, re-registered before any B run; rule H.
